$schema-note: Owner Writing Rule Enforcement & Model Answer Validation Addendum, Revision 8 (11 Sep 2026; Revision 7 content = §13 of the same PDF). Canonical registry additions OWN-W-001..OWN-W-038, applied to every Writing profession. 'model' = generated Model Answer (stricter canonical house style, every violation blocks publication); 'candidate' = candidate grading (professional alternatives and semantic equivalents accepted; Model Answer similarity contributes ZERO). check_ids are WritingRuleEngine detector ids (deterministic enforcement); rules with no check_id are enforced by the AI grader + the independent semantic Model Answer validator. Latest owner rule wins over older conflicting internal wording (Addendum §7).
letter_type_tokens: applies_to uses the legacy tokens WritingLetterTypeTaxonomy.ToLegacyLetterType produces (routine_referral, urgent_referral, discharge, transfer_letter, non_medical_referral, other_letters); every consumer normalises LT-* catalogue codes to these tokens before rule selection.

rules.title: One blank line after the Re: line
rules.canonical_rule: Salutation and Re: line remain consecutive. After the Re: line there MUST be one blank line before the introduction. Preserve this spacing in stored text, rendering, exports and candidate view.
source_refs: Rev8 §2 Blank line after Re: line
rules.good_example:
Dear Dr Still,
Re: Mr David Taylor, aged 55

I am writing to ...
rules.bad_example:
Dear Dr Still,
Re: Mr David Taylor, aged 55
I am writing to ...

rules.title: Salutation and Re: line consecutive
rules.canonical_rule: No blank line between the salutation and the Re: line; they are the only two consecutive lines with no blank line between them.
rules.good_example:
Dear Dr Smith,
Re: Ms Garcia, DOB: 1 January 1995
rules.bad_example:
Dear Dr Smith,

Re: Ms Garcia

rules.title: One date-format family and four-digit years
rules.canonical_rule: Use one date-format family throughout each letter (written, slash or dot — never mixed) and always a four-digit year.
rules.good_example: 13 June 2020 ... on 29 June 2014

rules.title: DOB written as "DOB:" + date
rules.canonical_rule: Write the date of birth as "DOB:" followed by the date in the letter's date family; never "D.O.B", "DOB 01.01.1995" or "DOB not provided".
rules.good_example: Re: Mrs Melanie Wright, DOB: 8 June 1973
rules.bad_example: Re: Mrs Melanie Wright D.O.B: 08 June 1973

rules.title: No brackets or placeholders
rules.canonical_rule: The final letter contains no round, square or curly brackets and no placeholder text such as [Name] or {Surname}.
rules.good_example: dalteparin, also known as Fragmin,
rules.bad_example: dalteparin (Fragmin)

rules.title: Descriptive numbers as words
rules.canonical_rule: Write descriptive/general numbers as words. Use digits only for age, dates, vital signs, investigation/lab values, medication doses and clinical measurements.
rules.good_example: every six hours for four days
rules.bad_example: every 6 hours for 4 days

rules.title: No emotional or editorial wording
rules.canonical_rule: Do not use emotional/editorial words such as suffering/suffered, unfortunately, fortunately, regrettably or sadly. Keep wording factual and neutral.
rules.candidate: unfortunately/fortunately/regrettably/sadly always; suffered only when used as emotional editorialising
rules.good_example: He had attacks on 1 June 2010 and 1 September 2010.
rules.bad_example: Unfortunately, he suffered attacks ...

rules.title: No judgmental disease or behaviour labels
rules.canonical_rule: Do not label a person by a disease/behaviour (asthmatic, hypertensive, smoker, drinker, non-compliant, anxious). Use factual forms: has asthma, has hypertension, smokes ..., reported difficulty adhering ....
rules.good_example: Mr Weir smokes twenty cigarettes a day.
rules.bad_example: Mr Weir is a smoker.

rules.title: Never "the patient" as the person reference
rules.canonical_rule: Do not use "the patient" (or "a patient at this practice") as a substitute for the person in the final letter prose. Use the name form or a pronoun.
rules.good_example: Mr Weir smokes ...
rules.bad_example: Mr Michael Weir, a patient at this practice, ...

rules.title: Name at the first mention of every body paragraph
rules.canonical_rule: Adults: first mention in each body paragraph = title + surname; children: first name; later mentions in the same paragraph use he/she/him/her/his.
rules.model: hard (every paragraph after the introduction, closure included)
rules.candidate: hard (body paragraphs between introduction and closure)
source_refs: Rev8 §2 Patient naming rule - exact operational form
rules.good_example: Mr Weir first presented on 29 June 2014 ...
rules.bad_example: He first presented on 29.06.14 ...

rules.title: Do not repeat the full name after the Re: line
rules.canonical_rule: Do not repeat the full first + last name in the letter after it has been used in the Re: line (the introduction included).
rules.good_example: I am writing to refer Mr Taylor ...
rules.bad_example: I am writing to refer Mr David Taylor ...

rules.title: No relationship label for a named patient
rules.canonical_rule: When the patient is named, do not use "your mother", "your father" or another relationship label as the normal patient reference; use the approved name form at the first mention in each body paragraph, then pronouns.
source_refs: Rev7 §13 Patient naming in family-recipient letters
rules.good_example: Mrs Ramsey will continue ranitidine, 150 mg twice daily ...
rules.bad_example: Your mother will continue ranitidine 150mg ...

rules.title: Model Answer opens with "I am writing to ..."
rules.canonical_rule: Every generated Model Answer introduction begins with "I am writing to ..." followed by the task purpose (refer, request, update, inform, transfer, outline). Candidate answers may use a different professional opening if the purpose is immediately clear; no template matching.
rules.good_example: I am writing to outline the medication regime for Mrs Ramsey ...
rules.bad_example: Your mother, Mrs Alice Ramsey, is being discharged ...

rules.title: Universal contact-offer closure
rules.canonical_rule: Every Model Answer closure, in every profession and letter type, ends with a professional offer to contact the writer, e.g. "Should there be any queries, kindly do not hesitate to contact me." Semantic equivalents are acceptable; candidate grading judges meaning, not exact wording.
rules.candidate: meaning required anywhere in the closure; any professional wording
rules.good_example: Should there be any queries, kindly do not hesitate to contact me.
rules.bad_example: (closure ends with the request only)

rules.title: Urgent closure: "at your earliest convenience" then contact offer
rules.canonical_rule: An urgent-referral Model Answer closure includes the urgent action with the canonical phrase "at your earliest convenience" and then finishes with the universal contact-offer sentence. A candidate may use any clear professional urgent wording, including "urgent"/"urgently"; never penalised for not copying the Model Answer.
rules.candidate: Acceptable Alternative: any clear urgent closure wording
rules.good_example: I would be grateful if you could assess Mr Taylor at your earliest convenience. Should there be any queries, kindly do not hesitate to contact me.
rules.bad_example: I would be grateful if you could urgently assess Mr Taylor's gout.

rules.title: "Urgent" only in the introduction (Model Answer)
rules.canonical_rule: In an urgent-referral Model Answer use "urgent/urgently" in the introduction only; the closure implies urgency with "at your earliest convenience". Candidates are never penalised for repeating urgency.
rules.good_example: I am writing to urgently refer ...
rules.bad_example: ... could you urgently assess ...

rules.title: Urgent referral: today/current presentation first, even if brief
rules.canonical_rule: Body paragraph 1 of an urgent referral is today's/the current acute presentation ONLY, kept as its own paragraph even when today's visit contains very little information; the next paragraph returns to the relevant earlier history in chronological order.
source_refs: Rev8 §5 Latest owner override: minimal information in today's visit
rules.good_example: On today's visit, Mr Taylor presented with ...
rules.bad_example: He was diagnosed with gout in 2000 ...

rules.title: Urgent purpose explicit in the introduction
rules.canonical_rule: An urgent referral introduction makes the urgent purpose explicit. Candidate grading assesses whether the purpose and urgency are clear, not exact template wording.
rules.candidate: purpose and urgency must be clear
rules.good_example: I am writing to urgently refer Mr Taylor for rheumatological assessment of ...
rules.bad_example: I am writing to refer Mr Taylor ...

rules.title: Hospital urgent referral: active conditions with current medication
rules.canonical_rule: In a hospital urgent referral mention every ongoing medical condition for which the person takes active medication, with the relevant current medication and dose (only from the case notes).
rules.good_example: Mr Taylor has hypertension, for which he takes ramipril, 5 mg daily.
rules.bad_example: (active treated condition omitted)

rules.title: Closure does not duplicate the introduction's request
rules.canonical_rule: The introduction states the purpose/request clearly; the closure must not repeat the same request wording verbatim. It may restate the needed action concisely where functionally necessary. The final contact-offer sentence does not count as duplicate-request wording.
rules.good_example: Intro: '... for rheumatological assessment of an acute gout flare.' Closure: 'I would be grateful if you could assess Mr Taylor at your earliest convenience.'
rules.bad_example: Closure repeats 'for urgent rheumatological assessment of an acute gout flare'.

rules.title: Linker vocabulary
rules.canonical_rule: Generated Model Answers avoid but, so, hence, furthermore, moreover and also as routine linking devices. Prefer however, therefore, thus, consequently, subsequently, in addition, in addition to this/that, or additionally only when logically appropriate; direct sentences are preferable to unnecessary linkers (normally no more than 1-2 per paragraph).
rules.candidate: hence/furthermore/moreover and clause-joining but/so detected; 'also' advisory only
rules.good_example: In addition, his brother has gout.
rules.bad_example: ... and his brother also has gout.

rules.title: Linker punctuation
rules.canonical_rule: At the beginning of a sentence capitalise the linker and place a comma after it (However, / Therefore, / Consequently, / Subsequently, / In addition, / Additionally,). When the linker joins two complete independent clauses use a semicolon before it, lowercase it and place a comma after it (...; however, ...). Do not apply the pattern mechanically when the grammar does not contain two complete clauses.
rules.candidate: hard (genuine run-ons/comma splices only; adverbial use never flagged)
rules.good_example: Her pain settled; however, she reported new swelling.
rules.bad_example: Her pain settled, however she reported new swelling.

rules.title: Medication-list syntax
rules.canonical_rule: Single item: Drug, dose. Two items: Drug, dose and Drug, dose. Three or more: Drug, dose; Drug, dose; and Drug, dose. Keep a comma between medicine and dose, semicolons between items and "and" before the final item; translate Latin frequency abbreviations; capitalise trade names, generic names lowercase; never invent a dose absent from the case notes.
rules.good_example: ranitidine, 150 mg twice daily; atorvastatin, 20 mg each morning; and dalteparin, 2500 IU by injection
rules.bad_example: ranitidine 150mg twice daily, atorvastatin 20mg each morning, dalteparin 2500IU

rules.title: Space between value and unit
rules.canonical_rule: Keep a space between a numeric dose/clinical value and its unit where standard (500 mg, 2 g, 1.8 g, 6.37 mmol/L).
rules.good_example: 6.37 mmol/L; 2 g; 10 mg
rules.bad_example: 6.37mmol/L; 2g; 10mg

rules.title: Age not duplicated between Re: line and introduction
rules.canonical_rule: If the age is already in the Re: line, do not repeat the same age in the introduction unless a specific approved exception applies.
rules.good_example: Re: Mr David Taylor, aged 55 / I am writing to refer Mr Taylor for ...
rules.bad_example: Re: Mr David Taylor, aged 55 / I am writing to refer Mr David Taylor, aged 55, ...

rules.title: Sign-off: professional designation only
rules.canonical_rule: Yours sincerely when the recipient is named, Yours faithfully when genuinely unnamed. After the closing phrase use the professional designation only (Doctor, Nurse, Pharmacist, Physiotherapist ...) unless the task supplies the exact writer name; never hospital, department, address, phone or email beneath it. Leave the approved one (at most two) blank line(s) between the closing phrase and the designation.
rules.good_example:
Yours sincerely,

Pharmacist
rules.bad_example:
Yours sincerely,
Dr A Reynolds
City Hospital

rules.title: Body 180-200 words (body only)
rules.canonical_rule: Body word-count guide remains 180-200 words, BODY ONLY (introduction to closure). Mandatory for generated Model Answers; advisory feedback for candidates.

rules.title: At least two body paragraphs
rules.canonical_rule: Use at least two body paragraphs, typically two to three; avoid one-paragraph letters and unnecessary fragmentation.

rules.title: No today's exact date and no "yesterday" in the body
rules.canonical_rule: Do not write today's exact date in the body (use "On today's visit"/"On today's presentation"); avoid "yesterday" (use "one day prior"/"one day ago").
rules.good_example: On today's visit, Mr Taylor presented with ...
rules.bad_example: He presented on 13 June 2020 (the letter's date) ...

rules.title: No contractions
rules.canonical_rule: No contractions in formal OET letter output.
rules.good_example: does not
rules.bad_example: doesn't

rules.title: Routine referral order and background placement
rules.canonical_rule: Start with the main complaint/current reason for referral and organise subsequent paragraphs deliberately rather than copying case notes mechanically. Place relevant medical, family, social and special-habit background near the end, before the closure, when relevant and permitted by the letter type. Do not include irrelevant background merely to fill a category.
rules.bad_example: Body paragraph 1 leads with smoking/weight/depression history before the presenting complaint.

rules.title: Discharge/update letter-type exceptions
rules.canonical_rule: The background-placement rule does not force medical/family/social/special-habit history into every letter: discharge/update letters may exclude family history, social history, smoking/drinking, previous medical history or occupation because the recipient already knows the patient.

rules.title: Professional clinical register
rules.canonical_rule: Use supported clinical wording rather than weak, colloquial or redundant phrasing (fatigue not tired/sluggish; MRI not MRI imaging; felt a popping sensation not felt something pop; does not currently have a GP not with no GP).
rules.good_example: reported fatigue
rules.bad_example: felt tired and sluggish

rules.title: The closure remains a closure
rules.canonical_rule: Management and history belong before the closure; after the closing request do not return to management advice (e.g. "She was advised ...").
rules.good_example: Mrs Wright was advised to avoid weight-bearing ... (body). I would be grateful if you could arrange ... (closure).
rules.bad_example: I would be grateful if you could arrange an MRI. She was advised to avoid weight-bearing.

rules.title: Introduction tense
rules.canonical_rule: Present simple and present perfect remain acceptable introduction tenses; present continuous is also acceptable when it correctly describes a current presentation ("who is presenting with features suggestive of ..."). The introduction stays concise and patient-specific with the purpose immediately clear.
rules.good_example: I am writing to refer Mr Weir, who is presenting with features suggestive of multiple sclerosis, ...

rules.title: Paragraph spacing survives storage and rendering
rules.canonical_rule: Address block, one blank line, date, one blank line, salutation + Re: line, one blank line, introduction, one blank line between every body paragraph, one blank line before the closure and before the closing phrase, approved spacing before the designation. The spacing must survive storage, API transport, HTML rendering and the candidate-facing Model Answer component; a rule-engine PASS with broken visual spacing is a FAIL.

rules.title: Factual fidelity and certainty level
rules.canonical_rule: Use only facts present in the exact case notes and task; never invent a diagnosis, test, treatment, dose, route, frequency, date or request, and preserve the certainty level (a prophylactic intention is never upgraded to a guarantee such as "will prevent blood clots").
rules.good_example: dalteparin, 2500 IU by injection to reduce the risk of blood clots
rules.bad_example: Dalteparin 2500IU ... will prevent blood clots

rules.title: Candidate grading: zero Model Answer similarity
rules.canonical_rule: The candidate grader applies the same source-of-truth rules but never uses Model Answer similarity, phrase matching or template matching; genuinely correct alternative wording, synonyms, professional phrasing and different valid organisation are not penalised. Model Answer similarity contribution to the score is ZERO.
